thread.title: Spotlighting the people behind Michigan's new tunnel entrance
thread.title_full: Spotlighting the people behind Michigan's new tunnel entrance

author: Drew Lenard
title: Spotlighting the people behind Michigan's new tunnel entrance
text:
Nico Andreghetto was pumped.
The graduate safety had spent four seasons walking down the silent, plain-walled Lloyd Carr tunnel before each home game. Now, in his final year with the Wolverines, his new coaching staff decided to renovate — and they wanted his help.
The Michigan football team added a live-broadcasted tunnel walk to its pregame ritual this offseason, equipping the Lloyd Carr tunnel with 390 feet of LED lights that send alternating waves of maize and blue beams up and down the passage, illuminating the players as they take the field. To go with the new light show, the Wolverines staff wanted their players’ assistance in finding the perfect song to play as they made their way down the corridor at game time.
Andreghetto and fellow graduate safety Rod Moore made it their personal mission, scrolling through their Spotify playlists and sending songs back and forth in an attempt to find one with the perfect vibe.
Eventually, Andreghetto sent one that Moore particularly liked: Joker and the Thief, a head-bashing rock hit by the Australian band Wolfmother. It’s one of Andreghetto’s personal favorites, and he especially likes the message it carries of an underdog “laughing in the midst of power.” To Andreghetto, that’s a fitting message for Michigan, where “everyone hates us.” Plus, he figured his coach would approve of it, too.
“Whitt’s a Harley-driving guy, so I think he likes it,” Andreghetto told The Michigan Daily.
Moore showed the song to director of game presentation and experience Jake Stocker, who’d also been working tirelessly with his staff to find a song that could be appreciated by the Wolverines’ entire fanbase. Andreghetto and Moore ended their search then and there.
The pair of veteran safeties solved the song dilemma, but there was much more to the tunnel changes than the music playing. The Big House’s pregame traditions hadn’t been changed in years, but Stocker and his crew took great care to create a new tradition that everyone — fans, alumni and players alike — could appreciate.
For over a decade, the pregame ritual inside Michigan Stadium has looked exactly the same. With just under 10 minutes before kickoff, the bell tolls on the big screen and the late James Earl Jones introduces over 100,000 fans to “The Best University in the World.” Once he’s finished, the horde of Michigan players waiting at the edge of the Lloyd Carr tunnel dart out to the 50-yard line to jump up and touch the “Go Blue” banner as the fight song blares. It’s the tradition, year in and year out.
But a new coaching staff often comes with new ideas. And very shortly after Wolverines coach Kyle Whittingham and his personnel first arrived on site in January, they knew they wanted to make the entrance their own.
“It was one of the first things they talked about as they saw the tunnel and pretty much said, ‘Hey, how can we create some kind of elevated tunnel walk that’s going to get our players really excited before they get down to the bottom of the field and hit the banner?’ ” Stocker said.
The iconic Jones video woke the crowd up before games, but once it ended, the players would simply stand on the edge of the field in wait for the queue to run up and touch the banner. There had to be a better way to carry that momentum into the moment they ran out on the field and into the game itself. There had to be a tunnel walk.
“We have this huge tunnel, and right now it’s just all white, and nobody’s really seeing what happens before the team comes out,” Stocker said. “How do they get hyped up, how do they get excited? How do we get the crowd into it before we hit that moment where it goes back to the tradition of the band playing, the team running under the banner?”
Multiple companies put in bids to be the one giving the tunnel its tune-up, but Stocker and his team went with 4Wall Entertainment, a national industry leader whose South Lyon-based Michigan branch frequently does work for the Pistons, Lions, Tigers, Red Wings and Wolverines. Just this past April, they were in Crisler Center putting together the men’s basketball team’s national championship banner-raising.
Over the span of three days in late August, vice president of live events, Joe Leahy, alongside his project manager, Kareem Harris, and programmer and designer, Mike Conley, brought a small crew in to install the 390 feet of linear lighting. The LED battens they used are capable of displaying any color in the rainbow.
“But in the Big House, we’re only going to do maize and blue, right?” Leahy told The Daily.
The crew also installed a couple EclProfile FS Leko spotlights that now illuminate “The Team, The Team, The Team” right before the players burst through the doors of the tunnel. Once everything was connected to the lightboard in the press box, the tunnel’s facelift was complete with enough time for a test drive.
“We were there when (the players) started walking through the tunnel and saw it for the first time,” Leahy said. “The parts we heard were reactionary, just them going ‘Ooh’ and ‘Yeah!’ Not anything verbal, but just their sounds.”
That initial practice walkthrough, though, was without Andreghetto’s song. Wolfmother only made its Big House debut at the season opener against Western Michigan, and Andreghetto was as surprised as anyone to hear it.
“We were like, ‘Oh shoot, like they’re playing the one that I picked,’ ” Andreghetto said. “It was pretty cool.”
The upgraded tunnel continues to be a success after surprising fans in the home opener, returning every week to carry the hype gained from Jones’ cameo right onto the field — just as Stocker had hoped.
Both Stocker and Leahy report it’s meant the world to hear nothing but positive feedback from fans about the change they helped bring about this offseason. It’s a tall task to try and enhance a tradition storied as Michigan’s, but by all metrics, the new-and-improved Lloyd Carr tunnel is doing just that.
summary: Andreghetto and fellow graduate safety Rod Moore made it their personal mission, scrolling through their Spotify playlists and sending songs back and forth in an attempt to find one with the perfect vibe. Once he’s finished, the horde of Michigan players waiting at the edge of the Lloyd Carr tunnel dart out to the 50-yard line to jump up and touch the “Go Blue” banner as the fight song blares.
